title: Pashas, edicts and judges
goal: Read the vocabulary of the Ottoman state, law and household, and recognize the Ottoman layer that law still keeps.

intro.text: Ottoman history and today's law share a vocabulary. A *kadı* judged in an Ottoman court, and a *hâkim* or *yargıç* judges today; a *ferman* was the sultan's edict, and *tapu* is still the title deed to your flat.

vocab.en: grand vizier, head of the Ottoman government
imperial edict; an order (ölüm fermanı: death warrant)
pasha (title of high Ottoman officials); today, a general
house, household (köyde kırk hane var: forty households live in the village)
mother (old-fashioned); Valide Sultan: the sultan's mother
judge (the Öz Türkçe partner of hâkim)

exercises.question: In a historical novel: *Sadrazam, padişahın fermanını okudu.* What happens?
options: The grand vizier reads out the sultan's edict
The sultan reads out the grand vizier's letter
A judge reads out a verdict

why.1: *Sadrazam* is the subject, and the genitive *padişahın* makes the edict the sultan's.
why.2: A judge would be a *kadı*, and a verdict a *hüküm*.
why.3: No pasha here: the *sadrazam* is the grand vizier.

exercises.explain: *Sadrazam* (grand vizier) is the subject; *padişahın fermanını* (the sultan's edict) is the object.

exercises.text: Osmanlı'da davalara ___ bakardı; bugün hâkim ya da ___ bakıyor.
exercises.en: In Ottoman times a kadi heard the cases; today a judge does.
exercises.hint: The second blank is the Öz Türkçe partner of *hâkim*.
exercises.explain: The *kadı* was the Ottoman judge; today's courts have a *hâkim*, also called *yargıç*.

accept: The title deed of this house is in my grandfather's name.
The title deed of this house is in my grandpa's name
The title deed to this house is in my [grandfather's|grandpa's] name
The title deed for this house is in my [grandfather's|grandpa's] name
The deed [of|to|for] this house is in my [grandfather's|grandpa's] name
This house's [title deed|deed] is in my [grandfather's|grandpa's] name
This house is [in|registered in] my [grandfather's|grandpa's] name
exercises.explain: *Tapu* (title deed) is a legal word that never changed; *dedemin adına* is **in my grandfather's name**.

exercises.prompt: The witness didn't come to court.
exercises.explain: *Tanık* is the word of the courts; *şahit*, which TDK sends to *tanık*, is common in speech.

exercises.question: A friend writes: *Pederim sana selam söyledi.* How does *pederim* sound?
options: Playfully formal, like an old-fashioned gentleman

why.1: Nothing rude: *peder* is a respectful old word.
why.3: Children say *babam*; *peder* is the opposite of childish.

exercises.explain: *Peder* is an old Persian word for **father**. Said today, *pederim* is a small joke about sounding formal.

exercises.title: Bir konağın hikâyesi
exercises.passage:
Mahallemizdeki büyük konak, on dokuzuncu yüzyılda bir paşa için yapılmış. Paşa ölünce konak oğluna, sonra torunlarına kalmış. O zamanlar evde, hizmetçilerle birlikte otuz kişilik bir hane yaşarmış; paşanın annesi, ev halkının “valide hanımı”, en üst katta otururmuş.

1920'lerden sonra aile dağılmış, konak yıllarca boş kalmış. Torunlardan biri konağın bir vakıf tarafından korunmasını istemiş, ama tapuda başka bir kardeşin de adı varmış ve mesele mahkemeye gitmiş. Hâkim, iki tarafın tanıklarını dinledikten sonra konağın vakfa verilmesine karar vermiş.

Bugün konak bir kütüphane. Dedem şöyle diyor: “Benim çocukluğumda bu kapıdan kimse giremezdi; şimdi herkes burada kitap okuyor.”

glossary.en: household, the people of a house

exercises.translation: The big mansion in our neighbourhood was built for a pasha in the 19th century, so the story goes. When the pasha died, the mansion passed to his son, then to his grandchildren. In those days a household of thirty, servants included, lived in the house; the pasha's mother, the household's 'valide hanım', lived on the top floor. After the 1920s the family scattered, and the mansion stood empty for years. One of the grandchildren wanted a foundation to look after it, but another sibling's name was also on the title deed, and the matter went to court. After hearing both sides' witnesses, the judge decided that the mansion should go to the foundation. Today the mansion is a library. My grandfather says: 'In my childhood nobody could go through this door; now everyone reads books here.'

questions.q: Why are the first two paragraphs told in `-mIş`?
options: The narrator was told the story and didn't see it
The narrator thinks it is false
questions.explain: Local and family history from before the narrator's time is told in `-mIş` ([C2 unit 2](gp-narrative-tenses)).

questions.q: Why did the matter go to court?
options: Another sibling's name was also on the title deed
A judge, after hearing both sides' witnesses

questions.q: Which word in the text is a legal term still in use today?
questions.explain: *Tapu*, the title deed, is the word of today's land registry; *paşa* and *valide hanım* belong to the Ottoman household.

exercises.text: Dedem “Bu vilayetin valisi” derdi; biz bugün “Bu ___ valisi” diyoruz.
exercises.en: My grandfather used to say 'the governor of this vilayet'; today we say 'the governor of this province'.
exercises.explain: TDK sends *vilayet* to *il*, today's word for a province; its governor is still the *vali*.

exercises.en: The grand vizier read out the sultan's edict.

exercises.task: Translate this episode summary of a historical series into natural English. Glosses: *konaklamak* to stop for the night, *çağırtmak* to send for, to have someone brought.
exercises.source: Sadrazam, padişahın fermanını vilayete götürmek için yola çıkar. Yolda bir köyde konaklar. Köyün kadısı, bir vakfın tapusu yüzünden çıkan kavgayı çözemez. Sadrazam iki tarafı dinler, tanıkları çağırtır ve hükmünü verir.
models: The grand vizier sets off to take the sultan's edict to the province. On the way, he stops for the night in a village. The village kadi cannot settle a quarrel over a foundation's title deed. The grand vizier hears both sides, sends for the witnesses and gives his verdict.

The grand vizier leaves to deliver the sultan's decree to the province, stopping for the night in a village on the way. There the local judge is unable to resolve a dispute over the title deed of a foundation, so the grand vizier listens to both sides, has the witnesses brought in and pronounces judgment.
checklist: The summary stays in the present tense, as in Turkish
*sadrazam* comes out as **grand vizier**, *kadı* as **kadi** or **judge**
*çağırtır* is causative: he **sends for** the witnesses or **has them brought**
